MODAL_COULD.text: A community center kept a freezer for donated food. Part of the food was for families who needed help that week, and part was emergency stock for storms. In August, volunteers noticed that several meals had passed their best-use dates while other shelves became almost empty. A group of students studied the freezer log instead of simply asking for more donations. The log recorded the date, food type, number of packs, and whether each pack was marked ‘weekly' or ‘emergency.' The students found two patterns. First, new weekly donations were often placed in front of older ones, so volunteers took the newest packs first. Second, emergency stock was checked only once a month, which made it easy to miss items that were close to their dates. The students suggested three changes. Older weekly packs would be placed in a clearly marked front basket. Emergency food would still be protected, but volunteers would check its dates every week and replace near-date packs with newer ones. Finally, the center would write the number of available weekly packs on a small board before accepting extra donations of the same kind. After six weeks, the freezer still held the required emergency amount, but fewer meals were thrown away. The students did not reduce the safety stock. They used the same records more carefully to balance immediate needs and future emergencies. The center kept the old procedure in the file too, so future volunteers could compare the results and understand why the new system had been adopted.

MODAL_CAN.text: The science museum asked a student team to check a new bilingual safety notice. The English notice said visitors could touch the model only when a staff member was present. The Japanese version, however, simply said that visitors could touch the model. Yui first wondered whether the shorter translation was intentional. She compared it with an older notice and then asked the museum educator. The educator explained that the condition was important because one part of the model became hot during demonstrations. The team rewrote the Japanese sentence so that the condition about staff presence was clear. They also checked the other five rules line by line, rather than assuming that the rest were correct because they looked similar. No other meaning was missing. Before the notice was printed, another student read only the Japanese version and correctly explained when touching was allowed. The team learned that a translation can contain almost all the right words and still change a safety rule if one condition disappears.

MODAL_COULD.text: The city planned a weekend river festival, and a junior-high volunteer team was asked to prepare a route guide for visitors arriving at Midori Station. Usually, the shortest walk from the station to the festival field followed the east river path. However, part of that path would be closed for bridge repairs on Saturday morning. The first draft of the guide simply told everyone to use the west path instead. Rina thought that advice was safe but not complete because visitors would arrive at different times and some would come by bus. The team gathered three pieces of information. The route map showed that the normal east path was 1.2 kilometers, the west walking route was 1.7 kilometers, and a third route used a bus from the station to Library Stop followed by a 0.5-kilometer walk. The construction table said the east path between Bridge A and Gate 2 would be closed from 8:30 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. After 11:30, the path would reopen, but bicycles would still be prohibited until 2:00 p.m. The bus schedule showed departures from Midori Station at 8:40, 9:10, 9:40, 10:40, and 11:40. The ride to Library Stop took eight minutes. The team tested three example visitors. A family arriving at 9:00 with a small child could take the 9:10 bus and avoid the longer west walk. A walking club arriving at 10:15 could use the west route immediately instead of waiting twenty-five minutes for the next bus. A visitor arriving at noon could use the reopened east path, which was again the shortest walking route. These examples showed why one fixed instruction would not help everyone. The final board began with a clear warning about the 8:30–11:30 closure. Under it, the team added a simple choice: before 11:30, use the west walk or check the next bus; after 11:30, walkers may use the east path again. A bicycle symbol remained crossed out until 2:00. The board did not claim that one route was always best. It connected the map, the time of arrival, and the transport schedule so visitors could make a safe choice for their own situation.

MODAL_MAY_MIGHT.text: The school newspaper was preparing an article about a new community sports park. A reporter found a strong quote in an old interview file: ‘We expect the park to open next spring.' The sentence fit the article, so the first draft used it without a date. Before publication, Akira checked when the interview had been recorded. It was from eighteen months earlier. Since then, construction had been delayed twice, and the current city page listed a different opening season. The reporter did not delete the quote because it still showed what planners had expected at that time. Instead, the article identified the interview date and added the current schedule in the next sentence. The team also checked two other quotations whose timing might affect their meaning. Those dates were already clear. By adding one missing date, the newspaper avoided making an old expectation sound like a current promise. That context mattered.

MODAL_CAN.text: A nature club surveyed birds in a riverside park and found two very different results. On Tuesday morning, one team counted forty-two small birds. On Thursday evening, another team counted only twenty-six. At first, several students said the birds must leave the park later in the day. Mika was not sure. She compared the survey sheets and found three other differences. The morning team had walked the north path, where many berry bushes grew. The evening team had used the south path beside the sports field. Tuesday had been cool and cloudy, while Thursday had been warm and windy. The two teams had also counted for different lengths of time. To test the idea more fairly, the club repeated the survey twice the following week. Both teams used the same north path for thirty minutes. One survey began at 7:30 a.m. and the other at 5:30 p.m. The morning count was thirty-six and the evening count was thirty-two, a much smaller difference than before. The students could not conclude that time had no effect, but they also could not claim that it explained the first large gap. In their report, they listed time, weather, route, and counting area as factors that had changed. They included all four counts instead of choosing only the numbers that supported their first idea. The club learned that two measurements can look comparable while being taken under conditions that are not actually the same.

WILL_FUTURE.text: Class 3-2 was planning a museum visit for forty students and four adults. The museum required school groups to reserve entry times for three popular rooms. The class wanted to see all three before lunch, but the first plan did not fit the rules. Instead of guessing, the planning team put the capacity table, timed-entry card, and floor guide next to one another. The capacity table listed Local Life Room: 24 people, Industry Room: 30 people, and Special Gallery: 20 people. The timed-entry card offered starting times at 10:00, 10:40, and 11:20. A group needed about thirty minutes in each room, and the museum allowed no more than two school groups to begin at the same time. The floor guide showed that Local Life and Industry were on the first floor. The Special Gallery was upstairs, and walking there from either first-floor room took about seven minutes. The class lunch reservation was at 12:20 in a hall beside the entrance. Everyone needed to be back there by 12:10. The first draft divided the class into two groups of twenty-two. At 10:00, Group A would enter Local Life and Group B would enter Industry. At 10:40, both groups would exchange rooms. At 11:20, they would both enter the Special Gallery. That final step was impossible because forty-four people could not enter a room with capacity twenty. The team considered making three groups, but the timed-entry rule created another problem. Three groups could not all start a reserved room at 10:00. So the students kept two groups but changed the order. Group A, twenty-two people, used Local Life at 10:00 and Industry at 10:40. Group B, also twenty-two, used Industry at 10:00, walked upstairs, and entered the Special Gallery at 10:40. At 11:20, Group A split temporarily: eighteen students and two adults entered the Special Gallery, while the remaining four students and two adults visited a free exhibit nearby. Group B used Local Life at 11:20. The small group from A could visit the free exhibit first and then join the others after the reserved room. The revised plan was not perfectly equal, but it satisfied every capacity and starting-time rule. It also left enough time to return downstairs and reach lunch by 12:10. The students wrote one note beside the plan: room order may differ, but every student will see the same three main exhibits. By linking the three materials, the team found a workable schedule without pretending that one simple route could fit all forty-four visitors.

MODAL_CAN.text: The school newspaper received a photo from a sports day practice. The cropped image showed one runner far ahead while the others were standing near the starting line. A student wrote a caption saying that the runner had begun before everyone else during the race. Before publishing it, Hana asked for the original photo. The wider image showed a teacher holding a red flag and a board that said ‘Practice Start.' The camera time also showed that the picture had been taken twenty minutes before the real race. The runner was testing the course alone while the other students waited for instructions. The newspaper changed the caption to explain that the photo showed a practice check, not an unfair start. It also added a rule for future photo work: when cropping changes who or what can be seen, reporters should check the original image before deciding what happened. The smaller picture had not been false, but it had removed information that changed the meaning of the scene.

MODAL_COULD.text: Three wooden benches in a neighborhood park needed attention. Some residents asked the city to replace all of them, while others wanted to repair everything to save money. A student group collected information before making a recommendation. Bench A had one damaged board, but its frame was strong. Repairing it would cost 8,000 yen and was expected to add about four years of use. Bench B had faded paint and two loose screws. A 4,000-yen repair could keep it useful for at least three more years. Bench C looked better from a distance, but the inspection found deep damage inside two legs. Repairing it would cost 22,000 yen and might add only one year. A new bench cost 30,000 yen. The students also read user comments and observed the park on two afternoons. Bench A stood beside the playground and was used often by adults watching children. Bench B was near the walking path and was popular with older visitors. Bench C was behind a storage building and was used only twice during the observation. At first, the group thought replacing C in the same place would complete the project neatly. However, several visitors had asked for a seat near a large shade tree on the opposite side of the park. The final proposal treated the three benches differently. A and B would be repaired because their structures were sound and people used them regularly. C would be removed because an expensive repair would not last long. Instead of replacing it in the same low-use location, the city could place one new bench near the shade tree. The students explained that ‘repair' and ‘replace' were not competing answers for the whole park. Cost, expected life, safety, location, and actual use had to be considered for each bench separately.

MODAL_COULD.text: The city youth committee was helping with an outdoor festival scheduled for a hot Saturday. The first program placed all performances on one stage from 10:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. After a heat-safety meeting, the students were asked to check whether the schedule still made sense. They used three materials: an hourly forecast, a site map, and the performance timetable. The forecast showed 29°C at 10:00, 32°C at 11:00, 34°C at noon, 35°C at 1:00, and 33°C at 2:00. The site map marked the main stage in an open square, a smaller stage beside a row of trees, and a community hall with air conditioning. The hall could hold only 120 people, while the main stage area could hold more than 400. The timetable included a children's dance at 10:20, a school band at 11:30, a forty-minute local music show at 12:40, and a senior dance group at 2:00. At first, the committee considered moving every event indoors after noon. That plan failed because the hall was too small for the local music show, which usually attracted more than 250 visitors. The students then compared the needs of each group. The children's dance would finish before the hottest hours. The school band could use the tree-side stage, where shade covered most of the waiting area by 11:30. The senior dance group needed a cooler place because several members had asked for shorter outdoor activity. The local music show had the largest audience and could not fit in the hall. The revised schedule kept the children's dance at the main stage. It moved the school band to the shaded small stage at 11:30. The local music show remained on the main stage but moved from 12:40 to 2:10, when the forecast was beginning to fall. The senior dance moved indoors at 12:50. The committee also added free-water points and a twenty-minute open break around 1:30 so no group had to fill that period simply because the original schedule had used it. The students did not claim that the new plan removed all heat risk. Weather could change, and real conditions still needed to be checked that morning. Their plan showed a different idea: use the forecast together with shade, room capacity, audience size, and the needs of performers. A schedule was safer when the materials were read as one set instead of one table at a time.

MODAL_COULD.text: Residents of a community garden shared one water tank, but arguments increased during a dry summer. Some gardeners said every bed should receive the same amount of water. Others said the sunny beds needed more. A student science group offered to study the problem for two weeks. The garden had twelve beds. Six were in full sun for most of the afternoon, and six were shaded by a building after 1:00 p.m. The students first checked the soil at the same depth each evening. They also read the watering log instead of relying on memory. During the first week, each bed received the same amount of water. By the third day, four sunny beds were dry before evening, while three shaded beds still had wet soil the next morning. The students did not immediately double the water for every sunny bed because plant type and soil were not identical. For the second week, they created two starting schedules. Sunny beds received a smaller amount in the morning and another check in late afternoon. Shaded beds received one morning watering, followed by an extra amount only when the soil check showed it was needed. Gardeners recorded both the amount of water and whether the soil was dry, damp, or wet before watering. At the end of the week, fewer beds reached either extreme. The sunny beds did not stay dry for long periods, and the shaded beds were less often overwatered. The students recommended keeping the two schedules as a guide, not as an automatic rule. A newly planted bed or a rainy day could require a different choice. They also suggested reviewing the log every Sunday so residents could see whether the pattern was changing with the season. Equal treatment, they explained, did not always mean equal amounts. A fair plan could use the same goal—healthy plants with less wasted water—while responding to different conditions.

MODAL_COULD.text: Two students saw a bicycle fall near the school gate, but their stories sounded different. One said, ‘The rider was going too fast and hit the curb.' The other said, ‘A bag fell first, and then the bicycle turned.' A safety committee wanted to describe the incident in a report without choosing a story simply because one sounded more confident. The committee asked each witness to separate what was directly seen from what was assumed. The first witness had seen the bicycle moving quickly compared with nearby walkers, but had not seen the front wheel touch the curb. The second had seen a bag on the ground after the fall, but had not actually seen it drop before the bicycle turned. A nearby camera showed the rider turning suddenly, but the view was blocked at the moment the fall began. The report therefore listed confirmed facts: the bicycle was moving, it turned suddenly, and a bag was found beside it. It described speed, the curb, and the falling bag as possible explanations rather than proven causes. By separating observations from assumptions, the committee could report uncertainty instead of turning two incomplete accounts into one false certainty.

MODAL_COULD.text: A local history museum tested two versions of an audio guide. Version A gave a long explanation at the beginning of each room. Version B divided the same information into shorter tracks beside individual objects. The museum asked twelve students to try both versions on different floors. They recorded how many tracks each student finished and asked which facts they remembered afterward. Most students said Version A sounded smooth, but several stopped listening before the long track ended. With Version B, more tracks were completed, although some students felt the story was less connected. The memory questions showed no clear winner: students remembered dates slightly better with B, while they explained the overall story better after A. The student team did not recommend deleting either design. Instead, it suggested a short opening story for each room, followed by optional object tracks. Important dates could also appear on the screen. Their trial showed that ‘shorter' and ‘better' were not the same question. The best guide could combine continuity with choices for visitors who wanted more or less detail.

MODAL_COULD.text: After a strong typhoon warning, a town prepared to open an elementary school as an evacuation center. A junior-high volunteer team helped decide how to move emergency supplies from the town warehouse. The warehouse had enough goods for several days, but the school had limited storage space. The students received three materials: a supply list, a room map, and a forecast table. The supply list showed 240 bottles of water, 120 ready-to-eat meals, 80 blankets, 60 folding mats, 12 battery lamps, and 10 large boxes of hygiene goods. The town expected about 70 people at first, including ten children and eight older residents. The room map showed that the gym could hold people but had almost no locked storage. A classroom near the entrance had secure cabinets but only twelve square meters of free floor space. A small nurse's room had power outlets and could keep medicine-related equipment away from crowded areas. The forecast table predicted the strongest wind from 9:00 p.m. until 2:00 a.m., with rain continuing through the next morning. A second delivery from the warehouse could not be promised during that period. The first suggestion was simple: take one half of every supply to the school. The students noticed two problems. Half of the folding mats would not be enough if most evacuees needed a dry place to rest, while half of the hygiene boxes would use valuable storage even though not all of them were needed immediately. The team also had to leave safe walking space in the gym. They made a priority plan. All sixty mats and all eighty blankets would go first because the storm could prevent another trip during the night. One hundred forty bottles of water and ninety meals would cover the expected group with extra supplies for late arrivals. Six lamps would be placed in different rooms, with the remaining lamps kept at the warehouse for other shelters. Four hygiene boxes would go into the locked classroom cabinets, and medicine-related equipment would be placed in the nurse's room near power outlets. The remaining water, meals, and hygiene goods would stay ready for a later delivery if roads were safe. The team wrote the reasons beside each number. The plan was not based on which items looked equally divided. It considered expected people, night-time risk, storage space, room function, and the possibility that transport would stop. They also marked the quantities as a first plan, not a fixed answer. If more evacuees arrived before 9:00 p.m., the numbers would have to be checked again.

The survey had been shared through a club leaders' message group, not with the whole school. That did not make the answers useless, but it changed what the results could show. The editors replaced the headline with ‘Many Club Survey Respondents Prefer a Longer Lunch Break.' In the article, they explained how the survey had been distributed and listed the number of responses. They also planned a second survey using several homerooms before making a statement about all students. The first headline was shorter and stronger, but it went beyond the evidence. The revised version made the sample visible to readers and left room for a better question later.

MODAL_COULD.text: A class project compared the growth of street trees using a city record from two years earlier. The old table listed trunk size, tree height, and location. Students measured the same streets again and were excited when several trees appeared to have grown very quickly. Before writing their report, Kenta checked the identification numbers. Three numbers from the old table were missing, and three new numbers appeared in the current list. A city worker explained that damaged trees had been removed after a storm and new trees had been planted nearby. One new tree stood only two meters from an old location, so comparing those two rows would falsely look like unusual growth. The class separated trees with matching identification numbers from replacements. It calculated growth only for the trees that could be followed across both years. The report still mentioned the removed and newly planted trees, but in a different section. By checking identity before comparing measurements, the students avoided treating two different trees as one continuous record.
